title: JavaScript package managers, dependency graphs, and lockfiles
concepts: Package manifests declare scripts and dependencies
Workspaces compose multiple packages in one repository
Install and clean-install commands have different lockfile guarantees
Package manager choice affects dependency layout and runtime integration

inventory.title: Mainstream package managers and their lockfiles
Dependency declaration and reproducible install commands
Workspace layouts, linking, and resolution strategies

items: npm began installing peer dependencies by default in v7; legacy peer handling differs
npm 12.2.2 is the current documented CLI; npm-shrinkwrap.json and npm shrinkwrap support were removed, and URL dependency installs are restricted by default unless explicitly allowed
Dependency install scripts are default-denied unless allowScripts approves them; strict-allow-scripts can make unreviewed scripts fail installation
Yarn 2 introduced Plug'n'Play as its default installation strategy; Yarn Berry also supports node-modules and pnpm-style linkers
The default lockfile changed from binary bun.lockb to text bun.lock in v1.2; older repositories may need migration
deno ci provides a clean, lockfile-strict CI install; deno install remains the everyday dependency install/add command and its target config depends on project configuration
pnpm 12.19.0 is current in the checked documentation; frozen lockfile edge cases continue to receive patch fixes, so pin the manager and keep CI validation

sourceSnapshot.authority: Official npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, Deno, and npm/node-semver documentation
sourceSnapshot.edition: Current package manager documentation checked 2026-11-17; npm 12, pnpm 12, Bun 1.4, and Deno 2.8 changes included

accuracyFacts: A package.json is a project/package manifest: it declares dependency constraints and metadata/scripts. A lockfile records a concrete dependency resolution (and integrity/source details depending on format). A lockfile does not alone guarantee byte-identical builds across operating systems, CPU/libc targets, lifecycle scripts, registries, or different package-manager versions.

npm 12.2.2 is the current documented npm CLI in this snapshot. npm install reconciles package.json constraints with package-lock.json: compatible locked resolutions are reused; a mismatch can be resolved and written back. npm ci requires a package-lock.json, fails on manifest/lock mismatch, removes existing node_modules, installs the whole project, and does not rewrite package.json or the lockfile. If tree-shaping flags were used to create the lock, the same configuration may be needed for npm ci.

npm-shrinkwrap.json is a historical lockfile mechanism. Before npm 12 it could be published and took precedence over package-lock.json; npm 12 removed npm shrinkwrap support and ignores such files. A repository upgrading to npm 12 should rename a project-root shrinkwrap to package-lock.json; package authors that need to ship a locked dependency tree should investigate bundleDependencies.

npm workspaces are declared from the root package.json and are auto-linked during installs. npm can run scripts in selected workspaces; workspace selection does not imply every command automatically includes the root package.

dependencies are needed by the package at runtime; devDependencies are development/build/test tools; peerDependencies express compatibility with a host package and are important for shared singleton integrations. npm 7+ installs peers by default, but optional peers marked in peerDependenciesMeta are not automatically installed. optionalDependencies may fail or be omitted on a platform, so application code must tolerate absence.

npm overrides apply from the root manifest to resolution of transitive dependencies and cannot freely override a direct dependency with a different spec; Yarn resolutions are Yarn's root-level override mechanism. These fields are not portable across package managers.

pnpm uses pnpm-lock.yaml and a content-addressable store. Its typical node_modules layout uses a virtual store plus links so packages generally see dependencies declared for them; files may be hard-linked, cloned, or copied depending on filesystem/configuration. Hoisted linker settings can change this model.

pnpm workspaces require a root pnpm-workspace.yaml (the current pnpm docs describe migration from package.json workspaces when absent). pnpm --filter selects packages and can include dependency/dependent sets using selector syntax; it does not mean simply running a command once at the workspace root.

In current pnpm, install is frozen by default in detected CI when a lockfile would need an update; explicitly use --frozen-lockfile for clarity and reproducibility. pnpm install --no-frozen-lockfile opts out. Do not describe pnpm's flag using Yarn or Bun semantics.

Yarn Classic v1 and Yarn Berry v2+ share the yarn.lock filename but have different lockfile formats and features. In Classic, use --frozen-lockfile in CI; Berry uses --immutable (default on CI) and retains --frozen-lockfile only as a backward-compatibility alias. Berry supports nodeLinker values pnp, node-modules, and pnpm; PnP does not create node_modules and relies on a generated loader/map.

Bun's text bun.lock became the default in Bun 1.2; bun.lockb is the older binary format. bun install --frozen-lockfile does not update the lockfile and Bun does not enable it automatically in CI; bun ci is the CI-oriented command. Migration of another manager's lockfile may happen in memory without writing bun.lock in frozen mode.

Deno maintains deno.lock by default for project dependencies and supports npm and JSR packages. deno install installs project dependencies and can add packages; depending on the nearby project configuration it writes deno.json or package.json. Deno 2.8+ deno ci requires a readable lockfile, removes pre-existing node_modules, and installs frozen; this is the clear CI command in the current docs.

Semantic version range describes a set of acceptable versions, not the exact version currently installed. A caret range permits changes up to the next left-most nonzero version component (^1.2.3 permits <2.0.0; ^0.2.3 permits <0.3.0; ^0.0.3 permits <0.0.4). A tilde range with a full version generally permits patch updates within the minor line (~1.2.3 permits <1.3.0). Exact pins reduce range movement but do not replace a lockfile or integrity/reproducibility checks. Prerelease matching has extra SemVer rules.

A workspace protocol dependency explicitly requests a local workspace package; exact syntax and publish-time rewriting differ by manager. Do not imply npm interprets workspace:* the same way as pnpm, Yarn, Bun, or Deno.

Package manager choice also influences dependency visibility, install scripts, peer resolution, cache reuse, native dependency handling, and compatibility. A lockfile generated by one manager is not a portable, canonical lockfile for all others even when some managers can migrate it.

npm 12 restricts URL dependency installation by default with allow-remote set to none; explicitly opt in to the intended URL source using supported project or command configuration. This is distinct from ordinary registry dependencies and belongs in supply-chain policy.

npm 12 default-denies dependency install lifecycle scripts unless allowScripts records an approval; strict-allow-scripts can turn unreviewed script attempts into installation errors. npm install-scripts approve/deny/ls/prune manages pinned approvals. This does not mean project-authored npm run scripts are blocked.
Deno does not run npm lifecycle scripts by default; deno approve-scripts reviews and approves them. This policy differs from npm 12's allowScripts and from Bun's trustedDependencies model.
scopeExclusions: JavaScript runtime API differences between Node.js, browsers, Bun, and Deno
